To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the conventional ecological theories based on contest competition, equilibrium, and the law of the minium, are not adequate for understanding the dynamics of many marine ecosystems, and that the dynamics of these systems can be better explained using the theory of scramble competition, transients and carrying capacity.
1) The three ecological principles on which the current conceptual basis for understanding marine ecosystems are based are insufficient for this purpose.

the dynamics of marine ecosystems depend strongly on the duration and timing of forcing, that the dynamics are dominated by scramble competition when the forcing occurs at time scales of a generation or more, and that the carrying capacity of a system is not a helpful concept for understanding the dynamics of these systems when the forcing occurs over a period of time that is long compared with the generation time of the dominant predators.

the conventional ecological principles of the first half of this century, based on equilibrium theory, are inadequate for explaining or managing marine ecosystems, and that we must develop new approaches to understand and manage these systems.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
variability on all time scales must be considered, and that the dominant dynamics in some systems is transient, and not equilibrium.
variability on time scales of less than predator generations, or of the dominant predator in the system, is not likely to be of much concern to the management of the system.
we are now at a point of transition in our understanding of marine ecosystems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the time scale of forcing and its position in the ecosystem are important determinants of the responses of the ecosystem to that forcing.

the conventional ecological theory that is widely applied in the management of marine living resources is likely to be misleading for many ecosystems, because of its failure to take into account the time scales of variability in the ecosystems.
we need to understand how the variability of marine ecosystems changes with time scale, and how this variability affects populations, communities, and ecosystems.
